stem: A client receiving highly emetogenic cancer chemotherapy is prescribed aprepitant as part of a multidrug antiemetic regimen. What is the purpose of aprepitant in this setting?

options.A: Prevent acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
options.B: Treat nausea and vomiting only after symptoms are already established
options.C: Reduce febrile neutropenia by stimulating neutrophil production

rationale: Current aprepitant labeling states that aprepitant capsules, in combination with other antiemetic agents, are indicated for prevention of acute and delayed nausea and vomiting associated with highly emetogenic cancer chemotherapy and for prevention of nausea and vomiting with moderately emetogenic chemotherapy. The label also states that aprepitant has not been studied for treatment of established nausea and vomiting. It is an NK1 receptor antagonist, not a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor or a mucositis-prevention therapy. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Recognize aprepitant as an NK1 receptor antagonist used with other antiemetics to prevent acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting rather than to treat established symptoms.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_locator: Full Prescribing Information §1.1 Prevention of Chemotherapy Induced Nausea and Vomiting (CINV): in combination with other antiemetic agents, prevention of acute and delayed nausea/vomiting with highly emetogenic chemotherapy and prevention with moderately emetogenic chemotherapy; §1.3 Limitations of Use: not studied for treatment of established nausea and vomiting
source_claim_supported: Aprepitant is used with other antiemetics to prevent acute and delayed CINV in specified chemotherapy settings and is not established for treatment of nausea/vomiting after symptoms are already present.

correction_summary: Replaced the broad source wording with the exact current labeled indication: aprepitant is used in combination with other antiemetic agents to prevent acute and delayed CINV. Added the current label limitation that it has not been studied for treatment of established nausea/vomiting and replaced weak distractors with distinct medication-purpose alternatives.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by the current 2026 DailyMed label. B conflicts with the explicit limitation of use. C describes a G-CSF indication such as filgrastim, and D describes a different supportive-care construct. The stem specifies highly emetogenic chemotherapy and multidrug antiemetic use, so the labeled context is explicit. No dose, timing, or unsupported efficacy magnitude is asserted. One best answer remains with no second-answer, cueing, or overlap problem. NCSBN 2026 mapping is direct.
